speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
The Porte Dauphine, our small great lakes research vessel, while not an icebreaker can work in light ice and has been sent up from lake Ontario to the lakehead to assist in this connection. subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON TRIAL OF CANADIAN CITIZEN
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Will the minister report to the house on the procedure followed by the Czechoslovakian government during the trial of a Czech born Canadian citizen, and whether normal international practice was followed in that case?

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of Slate for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON TRIAL OF CANADIAN CITIZEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Milorad Cop, a Canadian citizen who was born in Prague, was arrested by the Czechoslovak authorities late in July while on a private visit to Czechoslovakia. He was held incommunicado for almost four months and was brought to trial November 9. The result, which was pronounced on November 10, was that he had been found guilty of spying on behalf of a foreign power and was sentenced to seven years in prison. It is understood that Mr. Cop's defence lawyer is lodging an appeal.
The Canadian government has received no information beyond this about the trial or about the specific charges made against Mr. Cop. The Czechoslovak authorities refused to allow the Canadian legation in Prague to be represented at the trial, although an observer was present when the sentence was announced. The Canadian government cannot therefore express any opinion as to whether Mr. Cop was given a fair trial.
In the interval between Mr. Cop's arrest and his trial, repeated efforts were made by the Canadian legation to obtain an interview with Mr. Cop. The Czechoslovak authorities consistently refused to allow such an interview, thus refusing to honour what is normal diplomatic practice in such matters.
At various times between the arrest of Mr. Cop and his trial, the Czech authorities have been made aware of the dissatisfaction of the Canadian government at the refusal to allow the normal consular access to this Canadian citizen. Our views have been made abundantly clear to the Czech authorities by calling in the Czechoslovak minister to Canada and by having the Canadian minister to Czechoslovakia speak at a high level to the foreign ministry in Prague.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I outlined in great detail yesterday the effect of this bill. The

amendments to the bill itself should be noncontroversial; they are really technical changes, except for the last two parts, VI A and VI B dealing with sewage disposal plants and the universities. Rather than make another speech at this time, I prefer to answer any questions asked by hon. members.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to say a few words on second reading. I am not going to repeat what was said by my colleagues yesterday, except to say that I endorse their comments in respect to the amendments which will facilitate the building of homes for the aged and the provision for the ownership of homes and homes for rental purposes.
I was also very pleased to hear their comments with respect to loans to universities for residences. I was personally very pleased to see that provision included in the bill, because I believe that living in is a worthwhile experience in college. I had that experience I think, possibly, at about the same period in history as the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell). There are many interesting contacts made in residence, and I think a person who goes to university or college and who fails to live in misses a great deal. I could tell the house a good many interesting experiences I had at that time, but I do not think it would be proper on this occasion. However, I am pleased to see this provision for increasing the housing accommodation at universities providing for a greater number of students to live in, as we used to call it.
I am rising to deal with one aspect of this bill which is of particular interest to me, and which has been of interest to the Prime Minister as indicated by his introduction of a bill to amend the Criminal Code with respect to the pollution of interprovincial rivers. I am very pleased indeed to see the inclusion of a section to the bill which provides for loans to municipalities in respect of sewage treatment projects. I have been interested in the conservation of natural resources ever since I was able to think clearly about such things, and I have been concerned about this question of pollution of water, because our rivers are more than amenities, they are treasures which we should preserve in every way we can. I think it is correct to say that during the last 50 years we have been destroying these treasures wholesale from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and it is because the group which I represent is very pleased to see this provision in the bill that I rise to say a few words this afternoon, though I do not intend to take up the time of the house for very long.
National Housing Act
There has been a growing concern about this problem, as has been indicated by the representations made to both the federal and provincial governments by persons interested in the conservation of natural resources; by health authorities, medical officers, specialists in sanitation and certain groups and persons in Montreal and some other places where the study of the question of sanitation has evolved to a greater degree than it has in some places in western Canada and on the Pacific coast.
These representations show how laggard we have been with regard to this question. I was reading the report of a commission on conservation appointed, I think, in 1909. I read a report of that commission in 1911, and in that report I found a passage dealing with the serious pollution of the Ottawa river and the need for some immediate action to remedy that situation. That was a good many years ago, yet very little has been done that I know of to remedy the serious pollution of the Ottawa river.
I hope that as a result of this measure something will be done by the municipalities directly concerned and affected across Canada. This has been a matter of growing concern to several municipalities in the riding which I have the honour to represent, particularly to the city of Nelson, the district of South Slocan, the village of Castlegar and the village of Kinnaird. These communities are faced with pollution problems, perhaps because of the increase in population since the end of the second world war and growing industrial development. As a result of district concern a conference was held between these various municipalities and communities to see what could be done about this question. I was very glad to see that they took this prompt action before the problem gets entirely out of hand. The conference made representations to the provincial government, and I understand the provincial government intends to form a provincial pollution board which will have some authority to deal effectively with this problem.
In addition, the remarks of various hon. members of all parties during the debate on this measure indicate the growing concern of an increasing number of people in Canada over the increasing pollution of our rivers, and when hon. members speak in this house on this question it is obvious they are reflecting the opinions and concern of the organizations and people they represent. So I was very pleased to see this provision included in the bill. It is something which we in this group have dealt with over the years. We have urged the federal government to take action along these lines, and we are pleased, once again, that this government has finally seen fit to

National Housing Act
adopt in some measure a C.C.F. policy proposed throughout the years. I trust that the Minister of Public Works will continue to walk in the direction we urge and desire.
I have just a few suggestions to make regarding the administration of this part of the bill. I would think, first of all, that if the administration is to be effective there has to be a lot of public education as to what this pollution means at the present time and what it means in both the near and distant future to health and recreation. I think we have to get the support of municipalities and community organizations in the promotion of educational programs. You cannot give effect to legislation like this without understanding and support at the rank and file level. Without such understanding municipalities will not get the support for the bylaws that are required to supplement this legislation.
So I do think the first thing necessary is public education at all levels. Then I believe it is very necessary that we should have extensive research on this problem. There has been some superficial research by some cities and provinces. There has been some research done by one or two companies which are particularly concerned with sewage disposal plants. Beyond that there has been very little research either by the national research council or any other agency of government or by the universities with direct relation to the effect of the pollution of water or air on the health of the nation and the communities directly concerned. So I urge that the government use its influence to promote and stimulate, on both the federal and provincial levels, as a result of co-operation, the research which is necessary if we are to finally understand the problem and thoroughly inform the public as to the situation that we face at this time.
Third, I believe that to supplement this legislation which provides for the financial aspects of the problem from the federal point of view we have to have some federal and provincial control legislation. This is a matter so important that I think there must be some control legislation at federal, provincial and municipal levels. I apologize for using the word "I" so much. I am speaking as a C.C.F. member and for this group, but we in this group do consider that it is necessary to have some such control or regulation in order to give effect to the policies that must be pursued as a result of the co-operation of the federal and provincial governments in giving effect to this legislation.
I think, also, that this is a problem which is not going to decrease, because even though we were to commence immediately and even though we had some gradual success in meeting the problem, it is a growing problem because of the increase in the population, the

development of industry and so on. We urgently require some courses in our universities for persons who are willing to take this up as their life work, and deal with the problem of pollution of water, air, soil and so on in this country, as a crusade for national health and welfare. I suggest that is another aspect of the question to which the government should give consideration.
I do not say that our suggestions this afternoon are the end of all things, but we have given some consideration to the problem. Finally we suggest that to give effect to this legislation, to give effect to research, to give effect to control boards whether federal, provincial or municipal, and to ensure that their policies will be understood and that there will be co-operation, we must promote closer co-operation between the federal and provincial governments, the boards in question authorized to administer any regulations that may spring from this legislation, and the communities and people directly concerned. That is all I have to say on this question.
Again let me say that when it comes to the preservation of our natural resources and doing something to maintain for the Canadian people that great treasure of ours in a pure form-our rivers, lakers and waters-we support such legislation wholeheartedly.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Nipis-sing.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I cannot resist saying that I did not ever expect to experience any difficulty in being seen. If I may say so, it is rather refreshing.
Before speaking to the bill itself I should like to clear up some of the loose talk engaged in by the minister at about six o'clock last evening. I know he would not want to leave a wrong impression on the record. We in the official opposition have taken the position that the economic situation is serious, especially as so many of our people are unemployed. We are therefore anxious to cooperate with the government in getting its housing legislation through the house speedily. Proof of our desire to co-operate will be noted at the resolution stage, when only one speech was made by an hon. member of our party. We consider that early passage of this or indeed any legislation that may create work now or in the future should have top priority.
It was disappointing, however, to find the minister at six o'clock last evening attempting to twist or misrepresent our co-operation with respect to the passage of this legislation by indicating that it reflected an indifference or lack of interest on our part.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, may I point out that there are only 12 Liberals in the house at the present time, and this is second reading.

The hon. gentleman would do well to count the number behind him. I believe the minister's efforts last night were an attempt to cover up the fact that 22 speeches had been made by members of his party, which occupied the greater part of the two days of debate on the resolution.
It was equally disappointing to find the minister at six o'clock last evening, just as we were about to rise and with no time left at our disposal to rebut his statements, attempting to suggest that the former administration had done nothing in the field of housing in the period of 22 years. This indicated a complete lack of appreciation of the work that was done in this country in the past 20 years. This was a fine statement from a minister who would say on another occasion, when it perhaps suited him better, that housing should not be discussed in any political vein. This was an interesting observation from the minister, who has had the dubious distinction of presiding over an important department of the government primarily responsible for the greatest year of uncertainty and confusion in the house building industry which resulted from an inaccurate appraisal of the situation and necessitated changes and reversals of policy.
Surely it is hardly necessary to expand on the Liberal record in housing; the record speaks for itself. However, I believe that people are more interested today in the future than they are in the past, and in what this tight money, high interest Tory government is going to do to get this country back on the rails.
I should now like to turn directly to the legislation before us. As I said in this house last Tuesday, the official opposition intends to support this bill. We believe, however, that the proposed legislation comes too late to make a substantial contribution to employment during the coming winter. We also believe that it could be improved in so far as the cost of housing, urban redevelopment and municipal works are concerned. I should like to deal briefly with those points and make concrete suggestions which I feel the government should consider carefully.
This bill is apparently the main measure to be presented by the government to cure mounting unemployment at this time. In so far as Canadians may be willing to buy more houses, and municipalities may decide to increase their debt in order to improve their services, the proposed legislation will eventually stimulate the activity of the construction industry, but it comes too late to produce
National Housing Act
any substantial improvement in employment now or this winter, when such an improvement is badly needed.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I wonder if the hon. member would permit me to interrupt him. I am afraid that hon. members of the house are not able to hear the hon. member, a difficulty he has experienced before. I am sure the house would permit the hon. gentlemen to speak from the seat behind, where he would have a microphone directly over him, if he wished to do so.

Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. Not only am I experiencing difficulty being seen but apparently I am experiencing difficulty being heard. I was just saying that this legislation comes too late to produce any substantial improvement in employment this winter when such improvement is so badly needed. Indeed, this bill should have been presented during the last session. Instead, the government showed very little concern about the depressed conditions which were developing at that time. The government must take full responsibility for this useless delay and for the fact that the proposed legislation will not have its full impact when unemployment is most acute.
This failure of the government to act at the appropriate time is due, of course, to a lack of foresight. The government chose to ignore our repeated warnings from this side of the house and failed to see what was happening. We all remember the rosy economic picture presented by the ministers at the begining of 1960. I referred last Tuesday to the forecast made by the former minister of trade and commerce in his New Year's message when he said that 140,000 housing units would be started in 1960. But the bad forecasting record of the government is not limited to that instance. All the ministers were very optimistic about the immediate economic outlook. None of them, however, was more emphatic than the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr), who on the very eve of another recession, on January 29, 1960, made the following statement in this house:
What about the recession? Everybody knows that the recession is over. Everybody, that is, except those hon. members opposite, particularly the hon. member for Essex East and his group... I can well understand the frustration of hon. members opposite. They do not like this picture which shows that there is buoyancy in our economy and that we are out of the recession that they knew something about but did nothing about.
Those words may be found at page 517 of Hansard of that date. This statement is typical of the attitude taken by the government toward the economic situation in January, 1960 during the debate on the speech

National Housing Act
from the throne, although we were then at the peak of the cycle and another recession was about to begin.
Later on during the session when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) presented his budget he also showed great optimism about the immediate economic future. Here are just a few excerpts from that speech, to be found at pages 2670 and 2674 of Hansard respectively:
The survey oi business intentions released by my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce a few weeks ago indicates that this upward trend will continue throughout 1960... I am confident, however, that employment will rise as the coming of spring opens up new job opportunities and as the economy continues its upward trend.-
I expect that the forces of expansion will continue during 1960 and that the rates of increase we have experienced in 1959 should be maintained throughout the year. Within this framework I am basing my forecast of 1960-61 revenues on an increase in the gross national product in 1960 of about 6 per cent, or to a record level between $365 and $37 billion dollars.
At the time we were surprised at the assurance and optimism shown by the Minister of Finance who, we believed, had had the benefit of expert advice on the economic outlook for 1960. We were told only at the end of the session that the famous hidden report had been buried. The government did not only hide the facts; it buried them. Either they knew what was happening then and they did not tell us, or they were not realizing what was happening and if that is so they are not competent to hold office.
In 1958 they blamed us for having failed in March, 1957, to anticipate a recession that would start in the fall of 1957. In March, 1960 they themselves failed to see a recession that had already begun. As far as we were concerned, on the basis of the scanty information then available to us we could not share the rosy and unrealistic optimism of the Minister of Finance. Here, for instance, is what the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) had to say on April 12, during the budget debate. I quote from page 3149 of Hansard:
With a normal increase in the labour force this year the average level of unemployment in the current year might well exceed that of 1959, and surely that is a cause for worry and no ground for complacency of any kind.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: Will the hon. member tell the house whether that is the reason his leader has now declared he is going to bury the Liberal party's past?

I attach to that interruption the importance that I am sure other members of the house will, and that is nil. Before the

interruption I was quoting our leader and our attempts on this side of the house to bring the problem to the attention of the government early this year.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: So was I.

I should like to quote again. On July 29 the Leader of the Opposition renewed his warning. He said:
Throughout the present session we on this side of the chamber have warned the government about the unusual and growing level of unemployment in this country... We have been pressing for immediate, effective and realistic action in order to deal with this problem.
This quotation may be found at page 7226 of Hansard. Again at page 7227, the Leader of the Opposition said:
We on this side at that time, and earlier, warned the government against at least the possibility and perhaps the probability of a slow-down.
Throughout the last session we were accused of being prophets of doom and gloom-you have heard that monotonously, Mr. Speaker -and of misrepresenting the real economic situation for political purposes. Subsequent events, however, have shown that the ministers were those who misrepresented the facts. Experts now agree that the current recession began in March, 1960, but the government failed not only to anticipate it but to see it when it came.
This shows, therefore, that action should have been initiated then to cure mounting unemployment, and that the government could not have been more wrong in its assessment of the economic situation. As a result of its failure to see the facts as they were, the government decided to curtail construction activity and contributed to mounting unemployment instead of trying to prevent it. Several months have been lost, and the government must take full responsibility for the delay. That is why we say that the proposed legislation comes too late, and that it will do very little in the immediate future to alleviate unemployment.
I come now to the second point I want to raise, namely the cost of housing. We say that this legislation does nothing to lower the cost of housing. Conditions in the housing market have shifted radically in the last year. Demand rather than supply has emerged as the predominant factor. The minister now, rather belatedly, gives some indication of a glimmer of recognition of the existing conditions in the housing market. In order to encourage demand he is taking steps to reduce the down payment on National Housing Act houses, but at what a cost.
Here is what this government is willing to do for the little man they talk so much about. They are going to make it possible

National Housing Act
lor him to move into a $15,000 house for only $37,754. Is that not an extraordinary offer? During 1959 the average cost of a National Housing Act house was $15,000. Under the new deal the maximum mortgage will be $13,920, plus a 2 per cent insurance fee, or $14,198.40. The monthly payment at 6| per cent interest will be $87.32. After 35 years the little man will have paid out $36,674 plus his original down payment of $1,080, or $37,754. Of the $36,674 paid in monthly payments, $22,476 will have been paid in interest alone. So the little man will have paid $15,000 for his house, $278 to protect Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and $22,476 in interest.
I use this illustration only to point out that if the minister is really interested in stimulating demand for houses and in helping the little man to acquire a house, he will have to attack the major cost factor in housing today, namely the exorbitant interest rate which has resulted from the financial policies of his government.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: May I ask a question, Mr. Speaker? The hon. member is now speaking of the little man. Will he give us the figures for a $10,000 house, which would involve a down payment of $500. Let him put them on the record.
The minister can have his officials do that during the dinner recess.

It would not take too long. I do not have the facilities here, the adding machines, the paper and the staff to work that out at the moment, but I am quite sure the minister is well aware of these figures. He himself used figures yesterday; I do not think he should have any objection to my using figures today.
Will the hon. member permit a question?

No, Mr. Speaker. My time is slipping by. We can have a discussion in committee. Such an abnormal situation could perhaps be justified if we were suffering at present from extreme inflationary pressures and we wanted to discourage construction activity. But surely this is not the situation nor the purpose of government policy at the present time, when we are in a recession and when we suffer from a lack of growth momentum.
What the Canadian economy needs now is an easier and cheaper money policy. The money supply must be increased and interest rate should be reduced. But apparently the opposite is now happening, and the average rate on treasury bills has been going up, I understand, since September.
I should like to quote what the president of the Imperial bank had to say on this just as recently as two days ago. Mr. John S. Proctor, president of the Imperial bank is reported in the press as follows:
Banker John S. Proctor today blamed-high interest rates-for indirectly causing much of our current economic woe.
He urged lower interest rates.
He calls for a return to an easier money policy. This general requirement of our economy applies with even greater justification in the field of housing. Interest rates on housing must be lowered immediately, and I hope the minister will give this suggestion his serious consideration. Those interest rates are now at a record level. Surely this is most undesirable; this is the wrong approach, the wrong policy, if we admit, as we say on this side of the house, that we are going through a recession, or even if we admit, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) said the other day, that we are now experiencing serious economic difficulties.
I should now like to refer to the terms under which partnerships are established between Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the provinces for purposes of redevelopment. Here again the bill contains a provision which will represent an improvement but, in my opinion, it does not go to the heart of the problem. The need to provide low rental housing and to counteract urban blight is urgent in Canada. This is one of the most vital tasks to which, as a nation, we should devote ourselves, especially during periods of recession and mounting unemployment. If we really want to make progress in this field we must reduce the financial burden placed on the provinces and municipalities so as to encourage them to initiate more projects.
To achieve this purpose, the degree and scope of financial participation by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in those projects should, we believe, be increased. In February, 1958 the Liberal party put forward a concrete proposal which would certainly have had that result. I should like to renew it in exactly the same terms in which it was presented in 1958, and I now quote:
There is an urgent need to speed up the redevelopment of blighted areas in our cities. In order to promote this redevelopment we propose to amend the existing legislation to provide for a greater participation by the federal government. In particular, we propose to increase federal participation in slum clearance schemes from 50 per cent to 75 per cent and to provide for federal sharing in the cost of water, sewer and street services in the area concerned. Also we would propose to ease the present restrictions on redevelopment for commercial and other purposes as well as housing, where that is advisable.

National Housing Act
We on this side of the house believe that these two specific proposals, namely the increase in federal participation in slum clearance schemes from 50 per cent to 75 per cent and federal sharing in the cost of water, sewer and street services in the areas concerned, have a great deal of merit and should be included in the present bill. If we really want to make more rapid progress in the elimination of slums we will have to do something along those lines. I hope the minister will give those two suggestions some consideration.
The same general comments apply to the provision of the bill dealing with projects for sewage disposal and treatment. It is a step in the right direction but we do not believe it goes far enough. It will certainly be desirable under present circumstances to extend the scope of this provision so it could apply to a broader category of major municipal improvement projects.
In recent years a great number of municipalities in Canada have found it very difficult indeed to borrow at reasonable rates of interest. Indeed, access to the financial market has not been easy for those municipalities, which have found themselves in the same difficult position as small businesses. That is why the Liberal party proposed back in 1958 the creation of a municipal loan fund. Our proposal at that time was as follows:
A Liberal government would establish a municipal loan fund in order to make available additional finance on a long term basis for major municipal improvements. Readier availability of funds would make possible an immediate start on municipal works now awaiting financing and thus quickly provide jobs throughout Canada. It would help greatly to bring about a rapid expansion of urgently needed municipal services which in many cases have been long delayed because of lack of funds.
The exact scope and administrative set-up of this fund would be settled in consultation with representatives of the provinces and municipalities. It would supplement, not replace, existing methods of financing for normal municipal purposes.
A similar proposal has been put forward on several occasions since by the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities. We believe it is perfectly justified. The present bill will, in fact, discriminate against those municipalities which have neglected other local improvements to put the emphasis on sewage disposal and treatment. That is why we believe that our proposal for a fund to be used for general purposes would be more equitable and would do more to alleviate unemployment. I hope the government will consider accepting this proposal.
I should like to say a word or two with respect to the aid to universities aspect of this legislation. We in the official opposition are pleased with part VI A respecting loans for university housing projects to provide

dormitory accommodation for students. This is one of the several requests made by the Canadian universities in their recent brief to the government. I think all of us are aware of the great need to encourage and assist our Canadian universities. Our university capacity will have to be doubled within the next few years to handle the present rate of enrolment, and anything that can be done to assist is desirable. In addition, a greater effort will have to be made to encourage more of our young people to better equip themselves for the challenging times that lie ahead. Naturally assistance from the federal level must never encroach upon the autonomy of the provinces in this field.
The federal government realized some years ago that it was in the national interest to assist Canadian universities, so in 1951 assistance was made available through grants in aid. These were doubled, I think, in 1956 and were increased again by the present government. You will recall that further assistance to higher education was provided through the establishment of The Canada Council. At that time $100 million was set aside, half of which is being used to provide capital assistance for university expansion. We agree with this further expansion of assistance to our universities. Although it provides only for loans and provides nothing in the way of grants, as was done through The Canada Council, it should have a beneficial effect and we are pleased to support it.
To sum up, our view is that the present bill is a step in the right direction, and that is why we intend to support it. Our main criticism is that it is too little and too late. As I have said earlier, this legislation should have been presented during the last session of parliament in order to reduce the mounting unemployment that we now have. In other words, it will not have its full impact when it will be most needed.
Moreover, the present bill does not go far enough. I hope the government will decide to lower the interest rate on loans as soon as possible. Otherwise the benefits of the proposed legislation may be substantially reduced. Finally, I also hope the government will accept our suggestions with respect to increasing the degree and scope of federal participation in slum clearance and urban redevelopment schemes, and establishing a municipal loan fund.

Mr. Speaker, I most certainly welcome this opportunity to thank and congratulate the Minister of Public Works and the government on the excellent measures now proposed in this legislation to assist municipalities and home builders by providing additional money

to encourage many new projects both of a public and a private nature. The municipalities will gain the opportunity to instal long overdue public works and home builders, home purchasers, and home owners will all benefit from the availability of additional money. The general public will not only benefit from the utilitarian improvements achieved but also from the over-all improvement with respect to the problem of unemployment, one improvement which is bound to result from the implementation of the measures now proposed by the minister.
The part of the new program that deals with federal assistance to municipalities to build sewage disposal plants is, of course, the part that will be the most welcome surprise to the cities and towns of my own constituency, Jacques Cartier-Lasalle. I have just received my copy of Bill No. C-42, and I have not had a chance to digest it yet. There are some parts which I think will require clarification, for instance the part that mentions security by debentures. I do not quite follow how this will resolve in low interest, but I will not go into the details at this moment. We can clear this up later in committee.
I understand, however, that this assistance will also be extended to include the expansion of trunk sewer lines to take care of new or even old territory provided that the work is part of a general sewage disposal system. This will indeed be wonderful news to my constituents, who reside in an area which is probably more affected by water pollution than any other in Canada, if only by reason of the tremendous size and growth of its population and the utter lack of any organized efforts so far by the local authorities to solve the problem.
The abolition of water pollution was the number one plank of my own personal campaign in both the 1957 and 1958 elections. Therefore I welcome this opportunity to extend the heartfelt thanks of myself and my constituents to the government for this long awaited and long overdue remedial action. My constituents will also be glad to hear that the many letters they wrote as individuals and groups at my suggestion have helped in a major way to keep this urgent problem constantly before a very busy Prime Minister and cabinet, and I should like to thank them now for their efforts and congratulate them on their success.
The arrangement by which the federal government makes an outright grant of 25 per cent of the loan for work completed on sewage disposal units by April, 1963, is an excellent one, and should result in an early start on this work by many municipalities.
National Housing Act
My own city of Dorval adopted a resolution to take advantage of this offer on the very night the announcement was made in the speech from the throne. Dorval has also been in communication with neighbouring municipalities to see if they would join in a simultaneous effort to clean up the pollution of lake St. Louis and the other waters surrounding the island of Montreal.
It is hoped, in our part of the world, that the province of Quebec will shortly announce its own proposed legislation in this respect. I am sure the municipalities in my riding would be most grateful if the province were to agree to write off the remainder of such a loan in a similar manner to that now proposed by the federal government. This would leave about one third of the cost of sewage disposal plants and trunk sewers to be borne by the municipalities. I feel this would be a very fair distribution in view of the present state of civic finances. It is my understanding that $100 million is to be set aside for this purpose by the federal government. My own riding is certainly in a position right now to accept $2 million or $3 million at the proposed rate of interest over a term of some 50 years.
May I again congratulate the Minister ol Public Works for this very forward step, and assure him that this measure has my complete support.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to say a few words on this bill which is now before the house. First of all I want to say something with regard to the attitude of the Liberal party as it has been expressed so far this session. I do not intend, personally, to give up my responsibility as the member of this house representing Jasper-Edson. I feel that there are a few things I can contribute to the debate on this subject, particularly as it applies to towns of 5,000 and under.
I should like to put on the record, expressly for the benefit of the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Garland), the Liberal record in connection with housing in small communities. I have here the figures for the years 1954, 1955 and 1956, showing National Housing Act loans all across Canada in the small communities. There were 173 in 1954; 13 in 1955 and 375 in 1956. Now, if that is not a dismal record, I do not know what is.
I wonder if the hon. member would permit a question.
Yes.

Are those the statistics relating to all National Housing Act loans, including private loans?

National Housing Act

These are direct loans from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and if anyone should know you should know that the approved lenders would not go into towns of 5,000 or less. I shall deal with that a little later. I also have something else to say with regard to the housing policy of the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer).
Before I was interrupted I was going to say that one of the reasons we are having some recession and some unemployment at this time is that the Liberal party centralized everything in the large centres. They forgot about the rural areas and the small towns and the expansion that could and should be taking place in them. We have a recession now, and we have the Liberal press all across the country still yahooing about gloom and doom. The communications outlets in this country should be the leaders in showing the people of Canada all the opportunities that are available to them at the moment.
There are all kinds of opportunities right across the country. There are all kinds of opportunities in my constituency. There is absolutely no need for anybody in my constituency, because of the developments that are taking place, to be unemployed this winter. You just need to pick up the blue book of imports to see all the things we are importing into this country that we could be making here.
However, all the Liberal press can do is to preach gloom and doom. They should be ashamed of themselves. This fellow Neuman who was on T.V. last night should be ashamed of himself, and I will tell him so personally. He mouthed a lot of rot about things about which he did not know anything. A lot of these people need to take a trip across Canada to see what is happening. I suggest that our friends in the Liberal party ought to get out of Ontario and into the west to see what is happening.
The Grey cup.

They may see that, too, and as a member from northern Alberta I will even suggest who is going to win the Grey cup-the Edmonton Eskimos. However, if I might return to the problem that we have in our smaller towns, I would say that these are areas that are ideal for expansion and development. This government has taken some interest in these areas. I suggest the hon. members for Nipissing and Trinity should look at the direct loans made in small towns during the years 1958 and 1959.
You were in office then.

Yes, and look at the number of loans that were made. The total is up in the thousands as compared to about a miserable 500 in the three preceding years under a Liberal administration. I do not believe the income limitations placed on applicants for these loans should have been applicable to the smaller towns in our country because, as I have said and as I emphasize for the benefit of the hon. member for Trinity, approved lenders will not make loans in these areas.
We are also very appreciative of this reduction in the down payment which will be required under this legislation. I should like to point out to the hon. member for Nipissing that the little man does not have to take a loan for 35 years, nor does he have to take the maximum loan. If we are going to talk about interest rates for a minute, I would refer back to the famous speech on housing made by the hon. member for Trinity during the last session or the one before that. He discussed these interest rates, and what did he want? He wanted a relaxation of the Bank Act so the banks could raise the interest rate and pour money into housing. Now we have the hon. member for Nipissing talking about interest rates.
I know the hon. member for Nipissing was right when he spoke about a change in the housing situation and said that in certain areas it is now a demand situation. It may be true that 20 per cent of the new houses in the Toronto area are unoccupied. I know the market for new houses in the small towns in Canada is a good market. People will go ahead and wherever possible build new houses. This activity in the construction field will provide employment for our western lumber industry, and the employment will be provided immediately. Within the next two weeks lumber operators will be deciding whether or not they are going into the bush. This measure will provide the necessary impetus to get them to start cutting lumber. I hope, too, that some of our smaller centres will give consideration to low cost low rental housing projects, because there is a market in our smaller towns for this type of accommodation.
It is all very well for our friends to get up and talk, but they should at least stick to a few facts and maintain a fairly constant position from one year to the next. I hope when the regulations under this act are drawn up they will be broad enough and will not discriminate against those very communities about which I am talking, because it is vitally important, as I say, to the development of Canada that these communities expand and develop.

I believe that the step forward which has now been taken with regard to dormitories for university residences will be of particular help to all our universities. I am sure that this is the case in western Canada, because I have had representation from the University of Alberta that they would like something like this; they want something and will take advantage of it as soon as possible.
I want now to come to the question of water pollution and sewage disposal. In my constituency we have the start of a great water system coming down off the eastern slopes of the Rockies and flowing to lake Athabaska. We have the northern Saskatchewan river, the Athabaska river, the Brazeau river, the McLeod river, and the Pembina river, and all along those rivers we have natural resources which are just now being developed. There are new towns which have just recently been set up-Drayton Valley, Whitecourt, Swan Hill, Hinton. These are the towns that are developing in western Canada at the moment, and you will hear more of them in the future.
This is the kind of legislation that is going to help these towns to develop. It is going to help us to take the water resources in this great eastern Rockies watershed and make it pure and fit for human consumption in the future. This is the kind of step forward that only a Conservative government would take, a government which is interested in the development of the country and in conserving all the natural resources for the best possible use. The Liberal party would not think of this, because they would not be able to think where to obtain the patronage to carry out this kind of development. We know that the Liberal party could not do it, because in western Canada we waited 22 years for this kind of thing.
Therefore I wish to commend the Minister of Public Works for this legislation. I want to say to him in particular, again, that if at any time he feels it is necessary to encourage private lenders into the market he should remember our smaller towns particularly in western Canada. These approved lenders with head offices in eastern Canada will not go out to our towns, and in this manner we are discriminated against because we cannot obtain N.H.A. loans in these towns. I also want to thank the minister for this step in regard to sewage disposal and in regard to the purification of the water supply. I think it is a wonderful step forward and, as I say, it is a step forward which only the Conservative government would take.

Mr. Speaker, I must confess that I did not intend to take part in the discussion and deliberation
National Housing Act
today, but since housing is of such vital importance to every member sitting here I could not sit idly by and listen to some of these absurd statements and allegations which have been made this afternoon without taking part.
I listened with a very great deal of interest to the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Garland), for he has always taken a great deal of interest in this subject; he has always acted more or less as a speaker for the official opposition. I would presume that in his discourse this afternoon he expressed the opinion of the opposition in regard to this particular bill. I could not help noting, however, that there were two outstanding phrases that he put forward in his speech. Those two phrases were, "we, the Liberal party" and, "recession". He used these phrases to such an extent that the two became almost synonymous. I think that is what we are going to find, that the two are synonymous, and my reason for rising this afternoon is to speak on this very point.
The fact is that the official opposition all through its speaking and its press is always working to promote a recession. We find in Kent county that this is having a dire effect on the desire of people to either spend or not spend their money.
I must say that I was very much interested in the building that has taken place in Kent this year. The housing starts were to such a degree that the contractors were finding a great deal of difficulty in keeping up with the starts and there was quite a time lag for any one wishing a new home. I might say, also, that I was very happy that the number of unemployed in this district dropped to such a low figure this summer that it was almost impossible for the agricultural population to obtain the desired number of people to bring in the harvest successfully.
We find now in the terms and provisions of this new bill an extension of these possibilities, so that even more members of this particular riding are placed in the position that they are able to start, complete and eventually pay for their new homes.
I think in our deliberations we must always look to the fact that the people back in the ridings are concerned directly with their pocketbooks and with the way the economic position of the country as a whole affects them. In other words, whatever it is, they take this view, "How much will it cost me, and what does it mean?" With these restrictions now lowered there is the possibility that an ordinary working man will be in position to buy his own home with a $600

down payment. I think this fact will have a great deal to do with the younger generation of today becoming home owners.
We might just as well face the fact that the tenor in the last 20 years has changed radically in all phases of marketing and buying from pay as you go to budget and terms. As a matter of fact, it would have been astonishing 15 years ago to go into a store and have the assistant in the store prefer you to buy on budget and terms rather than pay cash. I think we must realize that the markets today have changed to such a degree that budget plans and buying on this basis is the recognized method.
Since there is only a definite amount of money on the market, and since all phases of industry are competing on this basis for the available money the home owner has to spend, I think it is very fine indeed that the average person today is placed in a position where he can think of a down payment on a car and a down payment on a home. The down payment on the home is so attractive and means so much to him and his family that he can also consider the down payment on a car. For too long under the former administration the down payment on the home was too far out of the reach of the ordinary citizen and so he used the money that he had as the down payment on a car. His hopes of owning a home were far away into the future.
I agree with the hon. member who has just spoken, that it is very hard indeed to follow the policy of the Liberal party. At one time they say the only solution was to lower the interest rate, and we have heard in this discussion and some time ago that the only solution was by raising the interest rate. I think this is generally to be found in most of the policies they have put forward. Therefore I would like to say to the minister that we in Kent county appreciate very much the step taken in the amendments to this bill, because it means so much to the ordinary home owner in the small town. Too often we forget the small towns because the development is so picturesque and can be seen to such a greater degree around the large urban centres. For this reason we tend to forget people in the communities with two, three, four or ten homes who are interested in buying their own homes in order to provide for the future of their families.
Once again, I would say that I am more than happy to support a bill of this kind, because it means so much to the people I represent.

Mr. Speaker, I take a great deal of pride in rising to take part in this discussion this afternoon, primarily because I am very much


interested in housing and, second, because I am very much interested in the amendments to the National Housing Act that are now before us.
I should be remiss if I did not take this opportunity to congratulate the Minister of Public Works and the government upon their interest in housing. This measure will not only put a very important group of our workers back in the field upon which they depend for their livelihood, but it will also be a great boost for an industry which has been in some difficulty for the last little while.
I have two or three points I should like to make this afternoon. I am very pleased with the provisions which would be included in the amendments to the National Housing Act. The one I am pleased with particularly is a proposal to increase from 90 per cent to 95 per cent the appraised lending value of a home. This will have the effect of reducing considerably the down payment on a home, and it will now be easier for a young couple to purchase a home with a valuation of $12,000 for a down payment as low as $600. Previously a home of the same valuation required a down payment of about $1,200. I hope a good many of our young people will take advantage of the opportunity to establish themselves in homes of their own very soon. This is a step in the right direction, and as far as I am concerned this provision will go a long way to assist young people in the lower salary group.
However, I do sincerely hope that the minister will give some thought to lifting the limitations on earnings entirely. I have had brought to my attention cases where doctors, pilots, skilled technical help and executive people wished to build their own homes but could not qualify for a loan because of these limitations. This program was designed to put men and women to work. The limitations have very little effect in practice because comparatively few people come into the wage bracket of which I have been speaking. Because of the intent of this program my humble opinion is that serious consideration should be given to lifting the ceiling entirely.
There is one other point which I have had brought to my attention during the last year and that is the question of direct builders' loans. I hope the minister will give consideration to allowing a limited quantity of builders' loans to each contractor who has in the past built a number of homes or to those who can provide or are in a position to provide the department with proof that they are interested in developing certain areas. I suggest that if a contractor builds as an example five different models of homes he should be allowed at least ten builders loans so that he can then sell or be in a position to offer to sell one model of the ten houses, up to five in

total, for immediate occupancy. I feel this is very important in the west and in Edmonton in particular where people have not shown too much interest in buying homes off a set of plans. This will also help the contractor in the matter of finances and enable him to keep his men employed during a slower selling period. I have a development under way in Edmonton East which could be speeded up considerably and many more men put to work if such loans could be made available to the contractors now.
The second point I wanted to bring to the attention of the house is the question of inspection. I suggest that a much more rigid inspection policy should be adopted. A stricter procedure-if that is what it is-should be set up with respect to the inspection of homes built under the auspices of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I have seen homes in Edmonton which had been passed by the inspectors but which were so badly built and finished that it is evident some means must be adopted to ensure better quality. I inspected one home recently in which the doors and the jambs were not plumb. The casings and trim looked as if they had been installed by a group of amateurs. The plumbing was not satisfactory because of the inferior type of the faucets and taps used. I suggest it is discouraging to make a substantial down payment on a house and then have to spend $100 or $200 replacing inferior taps, lighting fixtures and what not because the specifications did not demand a certain grade. One way of overcoming this problem would be, I suggest, to have the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation specify high grade Canadian materials or their equal.
Another point which has come up on occasion is the question of the lack of rental housing units in our smaller centres. I am aware of a considerable acreage where such houses could suitably be built. The acreage in question is in a working man's area in a small suburb on the outskirts of the city of Edmonton. The reason this acreage has not been developed is because of the lack of loan funds and lack of sewer facilities. Because there are no sewer facilities in that area the approved lenders will not lend. I am very pleased that some steps are now being considered in this regard. I make reference to the town of Beverly specifically, because although Edmonton has grown over 50 per cent in the last ten years Beverly has grown by less than 10 per cent.
Once again I want to commend the minister and the government on their attitude with regard to this question.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. E. Pascoe (Moose Jaw-Lake Centre):
speechtext:
The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) heard many words of commendation yesterday for the resolution he introduced regarding proposed changes to the National Housing Act and for the offer of federal financial help to municipalities in respect of sewerage projects. Bill No. C-42 is now before the house and I wish to add to those words of commendation.
I want to congratulate the minister on the very clear way in which he explained the details of the measure we are now considering. I can assure him that the changes in the act which he outlined will be well received in all parts of Canada. As he says, the changes will have the effect of increasing the amount of the loan to home builders and reducing the down payment. This policy, as he pointed out, will go a long way toward helping potential home owners to accumulate the necessary equity and reduce the need for second mortgages. It will stimulate home building and, despite some of the jibes we have heard from opposition members, some of this new home construction will be undertaken this winter.
I believe that the extension of the permissible repayment term to 35 years will be a help for some home builders. The minister pointed out that this longer term for repayment is not compulsory. It will, however, be a help to some young people who want to start their first home and keep their monthly payments as low as possible.
The silence of the usually critical opposition speakers indicates that they, too, realize the benefits of this legislation. As the minister said in his statement these changes in the act and in the regulations are being put forward at this time to support demand along a broad front. I have received suggestions for N.H.A. changes along the lines embodied in this measure. So, I am sure, have other hon. members. Those we represent will see by this bill that their suggestions were well received.
Previous speakers have pointed out that there are six main items embodied in this bill. Many have discussed the encouragement for home building in smaller towns and aid for the building of university residences. It is not my intention to repeat their statements. I should, however, like to deal briefly with the program of federal financial assistance to municipalities for sewage disposal and treatment as outlined in this measure.
The minister explained that parliament will be asked to set aside $100 million for this federal aid in sewage projects. Under C.M.H.C. two thirds of the cost of the proposed work will be loaned by the federal government, only 75 per cent of which will

National Housing Act
have to be repaid by the municipalities over a period of up to 50 years if-and I emphasize the word "if" because this will be up to the municipalities-prompt action is taken by them to start their sewage programs. As the bill points out, one quarter of the federal loan will be cancelled if it is spent on sewage work completed by April 1, 1963. To put it on the record again I should like to read from the explanatory note contained in the bill:
Provision is also made for a grant to a municipality undertaking a project of 25 per cent of the amount of the loan and the interest thereon where the project is completed on or before March 31, 1963. In the case of projects partially completed on March 31, 1963 the grant is proportioned to the amount of expenditures incurred by the municipality as of that date.
The minister stated that he has already received some inquiries concerning the commencement of this federal aid. I have also had inquiries from my own city of Moose Jaw where I hope the federal offer will be taken up as soon as possible. I have received letters from the mayor of Moose Jaw and from the city commissioner on this subject. Perhaps I may be permitted to read one paragraph from the letter of the city commissioner to illustrate the interest shown in this project.
We note by the throne speech that the federal government proposes legislation to correct community water pollution problems. Since the city of Moose Jaw is planning to rebuild its sewage treatment plant because of increasing pollution in the Moose Jaw river, with accompanying unpleasant odors, we are naturally very interested in any legislation which may be passed. Please keep us informed of developments.
I was struck particularly by one statement made by the minister yesterday. He said that any proposed sewage works must be approved by competent provincial health authorities. This is a very necessary precaution. But he made it plain, and these are his words as reported at page 94 of Hansard of November 22:
-it is to be understood that the province will not be the middleman here. We shall be dealing directly with the municipalities; that is to say, the federal people will be dealing directly with the municipalities.
I am glad that the minister made the federal government's position clear in this regard. I have found in the case of some dominion-provincial projects to which the federal government contributed 50 per cent of the cost, and in some cases more, that the provincial government somehow seemed to take all the credit for any benefits to the people. The minister has made it very clear that with respect to federal aid for sewage projects the province will not be the middleman. The minister went further and said, as reported at page 94 of Hansard:
[Mr. Pascoe.l
Whatever the provinces want to do besides this is up to the provinces. We shall be glad to have them make whatever contributions they can make.
That is a direct challenge to the provinces and I hope the premier of Saskatchewan is made aware of this challenge. The minister says he will be glad to have the provinces make contributions to these sewage projects.
I am sure the municipalities in Saskatchewan will be very pleased and very grateful for that assistance if the Saskatchewan government will put up a share of the cost in line with the federal government's offer. I go along with the Minister of Public Works in making this suggestion.
In conclusion I want to agree with the minister that all the programs envisaged in the bill represent a tremendous amount of employment, giving jobs to thousands of workers. It is one more line of attack by the federal government on the problem of unemployment. I am very pleased to support this measure.

Mr. Speaker, before beginning my remarks I should like to follow the course adopted by so many hon. members who have participated in this debate in extending my congratulations to the minister for introducing such important amendments to this legislation.
One of the most pressing problems in this vital field is property acquisition. Another is cost. During recent years, especially in the urban and rural areas, property has been bought up and is now selling at a premium. The situation is quite serious. People wishing to build homes find themselves having to build in poor locations where they encounter problems with respect to acquiring practical facilities such as light, heat, water and sewage. The expansion of municipalities has reached the stage where we now have to look ahead, not just to the needs of the next five years but to the needs of the next ten or 20 years.
In the rural areas where certain sections are being set aside for the construction of homes under C.M.H.C. I believe each company should be asked' to survey and set aside blocks, centrally located in the subdivision, for the construction of playgrounds, schools and the other necessary facilities required by expanding small communities. We now have to prepare for the future. There was a time when people looked ahead only two or three years but we now must look a decade or two into the future to the time when our small rural communities will eventually become urban communities and possibly large cities. There is a terrific difficulty, especially when loans are made available in the way they are at the present time. I should like to suggest, Mr. Speaker, that loans should

be available to all areas of Canada. There has been a certain amount of congestion of loans because they were being granted only in the larger centres and in the well populated areas. I feel that loans should also be made available to the small rural areas which are expanding faster than we had expected.
I quite believe that residences for students in universities today should be constructed at^an early date. The minister is to be complimented on his efforts in bringing this matter within the confines of the bill. In the construction of residences, we should take into account the newly married couple and also the single man and woman who are taking university courses. The buildings should be planned with small apartments and also apartments for single people so that the students can live in or near the university grounds. I am sure universities in general will welcome this venture on the part of the government and the assistance that has been offered. Accommodation for students in universities at the present time is quite a problem. A good many of them are spending two or three hours a day travelling back and forth from their places of residence to the university grounds.
The increase in the amount of the loan is also a welcome feature. I hope that at some future time all limitations will be taken off the ceiling with respect to the prospective builders of houses. This last year several houses have not been built because the prospective builders were beyond the wage limit that was allowed in the present act.
The sewage problem and water pollution have been brought to the attention of the government on many occasions in the past and little or no action has been taken. In the smaller organized or incorporated communities they have got by with a hit-or-miss sewage proposition. The day has long gone by where a disposal plant is the answer to the problem. So far this will not affect the smaller communities, but the preparation should be made now to build the plants so that this will not be a problem in the future.
I can see that water pollution is becoming a serious problem and will multiply in future years.
There is just one question I should like to bring to the attention of the minister and that is the necessary regulations under the act. When the regulations are drawn up I believe they should be simple and concise so that the average wage earner will well understand what he is signing. Let us do away with a lot of the little jokers in contracts and so forth which are in fine print at the present time.

Another matter that should be brought to the attention of the minister is the inspection of buildings. Since the war a great many houses have been built in Canada, and a good many of them without any building inspection of any kind. I believe that if a house is being constructed under Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation a qualified inspector should be placed in charge of the construction, a man who knows construction and all the various phases in the construction of a house from electrical wiring, plumbing and heating to the construction of the house itself. I have received many complaints from people who have had houses built for them and have found at the end of the job that a good many of the places were built with putty, plastic wood and various other compounds which were used to cover up a multitude of sins.
There is just one other item I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. I believe some assistance should be given to local groups who take on the tremendous job of building homes for the aged. I have one instance in my own area. Interested people banded themselves together to construct a memorial home for the aged and elderly people of my area. We have been endeavouring for quite some time to obtain some assistance in the financing of this project. Incidentally, the project is now completed and we are carrying a heavy debt over our heads. We have been endeavouring to have a refund of the sales tax on material that was supplied for the construction of this home. I believe we would be well advised to give local groups this advantage. After all, those local groups save the government of Canada a great deal of money in constructing homes. They construct them and arrange for financing all the way down the line until the home is finally completed. I understand that funds can be granted to a limited dividend company but that the local groups are debarred by national housing plans from participating in a venture of this kind.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I should like to support the other members of the Conservative party who are endeavouring to promote the welfare of all Canadian people through amendments to the National Housing Act, and I commend the minister on his forward step in this direction.

Mr. Speaker, it is gratifying to see that the government has amended the National Housing Act in order to promote housing construction and, at the same time, to encourage Canadians to become property owners. Those amendments should have been

National Housing Act
made years ago, especially when, under the previous administration, there were almost
600,000	unemployed in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I have here a brief which was submitted to me by the national Catholic unions of Joliette and I should like to read a couple of paragraphs for the benefit of this house:
The corporation should lend to prospective home owners up to 90 per cent of the money required for the purchase of the land and the construction of a family dwelling planned according to family needs and in accordance with building standards recognized in Canada;
Housing standards set up by the corporation should be made a little more flexible as a means of promoting the construction of a greater number of homes.
Mr. Speaker, that is to a large extent what the present government has just done, and as I indicated a moment ago, I am referring here to a brief from the syndicats catholiques nationaux. Here is what it says in paragraph 7:
Promote the construction of family dwellings.
Mr. Speaker, I would point out that according to statistics from every country in the world, Canada has the highest ratio of home owners, that is to say, 65 per cent of existing homes in Canada are occupied by their owners. Nevertheless, 76,000 more homes are needed in Montreal, and 100,000 in the province of Quebec. At this stage in the discussion, X should like to make a suggestion to the authorities of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation-perhaps it has been made in the past-to the effect that an investigation be conducted across the country, in every province, to determine what type of house the people want. So far, the matter has been left to the architects, engineers, accountants and manufacturers of building materials. Families would buy the houses they were offered, for lack of a better choice, and it would be interesting to know in what type of house fathers and mothers would like to raise their children.
A word of commendation is due to the housing co-operatives and to the caisses populates, which have been largely responsible for the expansion of housing in Quebec.
A case in point is the town of Joliette. A few years ago, the housing co-operative helped solve the housing problem and enabled a large number of workers to own their own home. Great praise is deserved by the housing co-operatives and also by the caisses populates for the great social services they have been rendering to the people of Quebec.

I was also greatly interested in this section of the bill which says:
Loans for municipal sewage treatment projects.
This act should have been amended years ago, to help remedy this situation and solve this problem. There are about 600 sewage disposal plants in Ontario against three or four in the province of Quebec.
The island of Montreal is surrounded by polluted water. There is not even a beach that is adequate for its population.
Water pollution in lake St. Louis is a menace to Montreal's development. I need not refer to the consequences of water pollution on public health and on animal life.
I wonder if a federal-provincial-municipal conference should not be called in the near future to study on a national scale the problem of water pollution?
For instance, in the constituency of Joliette-L'Association-Montcalm, the L'Assomption river is polluted. The water is also polluted in the St. Lawrence river around Repentigny and St. Sulpice, so tourists are kept away.
This is quite a problem to settle. I might add that oil companies in Montreal East should be wiser and contribute to preventing water pollution in the St. Lawrence river. You only have to go on the river in a small craft to see oil films on the water. It is not a very nice sight.
Let me go back to the magazine "Genie-construction" and its issue of October 1958 where one of the leading articles is devoted to the problem of water purification.
It is a question, of life or death in Quebec.
Says the author of the article, Roger Bedard.
A survey made in 1956 by Central Housing and Mortgage Corporation reached the conclusion that 68 per cent of the water in Quebec is a danger to public health.
Now here is a statement by Dr. Prevost, a professor of biology at the University of Montreal.
For a long time, it was thought that the volume of our rivers was sufficient to insure that sewage water would be diluted to the point where pollution would be avoided. It must be realized today that we are up against a gigantic pollution problem in some of our rivers.
Some of the most beautiful waterways in the province have become real open sewers, which are conveying a flood of poison to the majestic St. Lawrence.
That is why we should be paying tribute to the hon. Minister of Public Works, for amending the National Housing Act, so that municipal authorities may benefit from the legislation.

Our world today can no longer allow water pollution. There should be, at all levels, a joint effort to solve the problem.
I want at this point publicly to commend the representative of the riding of Jacques Cartier (Mr. Pratt), who is also mayor of Dorval, a progressive town of the province of Quebec, which took a step that might well serve as an example to all.
The city of Dorval took some action which, if imitated by the neighbouring municipalities, as it hopes it will be, will finally help purify the now polluted waters of lake St. Louis.
The municipal council has, as a matter of fact, passed unanimously on first reading a scheme for settling this issue which provides erection of a sewage disposal plant.
At the present time, Dorval and other municipalities on the shores of lake St. Louis are allowing their sewers to flow into the lake. According to biologists, the waters are so polluted, that from a sanitary point of view every year it is becoming increasingly dangerous to use it for bathing.
The mayor and-
The Dorval council know very well that construction of a sewage disposal plant in their city could not appreciably improve the situation.
Dorval authorities know however, that this legislation is the ideal way of dealing with the situation in so far as it is possible to do so.
In closing, I again congratulate the minister for his amendment. I strongly blame the former administration for its failure to consider this problem, for its shortsighted policy and for its refusal to amend the C.M.H.C. act, thus leaving unsolved the problem of water pollution, a problem of national scope.
