Mr. Speaker, it is with considerable pleasure that I rise today to congratulate the minister and the government for these further extensions of the provisions of the National Housing Act. The amendments in the bill are to be strongly commended. Since coming to power we have established a tradition with regard to national housing and I should like to say a few words about that later. I do not intend to go into the various details of the bill. As we went through the resolution stage yesterday two things were very firmly impressed on my mind. The first was the effect of the amendments on employment and, second, the effect of these amendments on the Liberals.
To deal with employment first, I would say that the changes being made in the act
National Housing Act
with respect to all forms of construction are going to make a tremendous difference to the Canadian economy as it is today from the point of view of providing work for people. First of all, with respect to housing, urban development, university residence and municipal sewage projects we have to look a little further than just thinking about what the changes may mean generally. In every type of construction you have labour and materials involved, and if you think of all the bits and pieces that enter into the construction of a house, wood, wiring, flooring materials, plumbling materials or anything else you care to mention, you will realize the tremendous turnover, not only of labour employed in the actual construction of houses but also of labour in the industries that supply the materials. Think, for instance, of the lumbering industry which supplies lumber for houses and the mining industry which supplies the metals to make other things that go into houses. There is no question that these changes in the act are going to make a great deal of difference so far as employment is concerned throughout the whole Canadian economy.
As I said, two things have impressed themselves upon me as far as the bill is concerned. The first is the effect on employment and the second is the effect on the Liberals. I want to stress this. I wish we could cure the Liberals as easily as we can cure unemployment, but that is not quite so easy.
I should like to make particular reference to the speech made by the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Garland) because, after praising the bill fully he then went on to make one or two comments which, in my opinion, do not harmonize with the fact that he has set himself up as the housing authority for the Liberal party. He used the words, too little and too late. He said that this was a step in the right direction. When you tie those two things together and then look back over the record of the Liberal party in connection with the National Housing Act you cannot help but wonder why he would make so much fuss at the present time. These Liberals are caught short. They are scared silly of this bill. It is good and, as I say, it is in the good old Conservative tradition. They must see that it will go through. They have to praise it faintly and find the only criticism they can make is these rather vapid utterances. Everything they say really adds up to this: It is a great improvement, but it is not enough.
I should like to refer to certain figures. When you receive criticism naturally you recoil a little bit and then you wonder what

National Housing Act is the basis of the criticism. I ask myself, is the basis of the criticism the Liberal party's handling of national housing up to the date of the election, June 10, 1957? Surely it cannot be that because if you examine the figures you will find that there was a total of $150 million devoted to national housing, of which $100 million had been used up.
No, $250 million.
Did I hear someone say $250 million?
Well, there was $150 million after you fellows came in.

Certainly, there was only $101 million used up by June 10, 1957, whether or not you are correct in saying that $250 million was authorized. I think if you look at the statistics you will find it was $150 million. However, apart from that, why was the $250 million not used up in all the history of the National Housing Act prior to June 10, 1957? In my opinion there was a very good reason for that. The Liberals called it a credit squeeze, but I like to call it tight money. The reason the Liberals know so much about tight money is that they had a naturally tight money situation prior to June 10, 1957.
And we have had ever since then, too.

Good show; keep on cutting in. I do not know how many hon. members went around to their bank managers or the various lending institutions during this time, but if you did you realized how difficult it was to obtain money. There was no possibility at that time of building a home. After the date I have previously mentioned the changeover was complete. This administration said that something must be done and they did something about the National Housing Act.
Again today the hon. member for Nipissing says that they advocated these things in 1958. However, in actual fact during all the time they were in office they did little, if anything. They did not even use the amount of money allocated under this act for national housing. The National Housing Act, in its original inception, was an excellent act. If hon. members will recall they will remember that prior to June 10, 1957 there was very little building activity in their communities. The builders, plumbers, and all suppliers were crying on the Liberal government's neck, but they were not getting anything even though there was a considerable amount of money still unspent in the national housing fund.
When this administration came into office we sold the people of Canada on the fact we were going to help them with national housing. We increased the amount of money

available. We increased it each and every year. As you know, this year we put in $500 million, and what did we do last year? We put in $300 million. The hon. member for Nipissing refers to ineptness, confusion and a failure to look ahead. He says we did not do enough in the national housing field last year. What a ridiculous remark to make in the light of the actual facts. More than $300 million was voted last year, and in addition the balance unspent from 1958 was made available. There was a total of between $330 million and $350 million used, and yet they say that we did not look ahead; that we did not do anything about it.
If you will look at the record with relation to the voting of the $300 million in this house last year you will not find one Liberal voice raised to say, this is not enough, you are going to run out. They said, you are not going to use any of it because Canada is going behind. How wrong they were. It is good to see the fund being used up. The housing fund is now up to $1,500,000,000 and on June 10, 1957 there was $150 million of which $101 million had been used up. At the moment there is well over a billion dollars out in housing loans.
Recall the big words used by the hon. member for Nipissing and when you hear the word "inept" applied to this government just compare the record of the Conservative government with the record of the Liberals in the field of national housing. Where was the confusion here? Where was the ineptness? Certainly there was none in this administration.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the minister, not only for all the various improvements in this act but for the very fact he is carrying out something which was started in 1957 by this administration, something which was started to deal with national housing in Canada and with the employment problem, and he is carrying it out in the best Conservative tradition.

Mr. Speaker, I know the minister will forgive me if I do not join in the chorus of congratulations. I may extend them to you, sir, because there is one aspect of this bill which was one of your favourite subjects when you were a member of the house. I recall that you were one of the first members of this house to request loans for university residences. I suppose you are taking a certain amount of interest and pride in the fact that this government has now decided to provide such funds. I think I might say that it is coming late in the day. The federal government of the United States has been doing this for quite some time. At last we have decided to follow their example. Of course, they have

had the same constitutional arguments against the federal state entering such a field as we have had here. But they have been in it longer, and I hope that some day the scale of our contribution in this particular field is as great as theirs. Several years ago-in 1957 I believe-theirs was $257 million loaned for this purpose.
The minister has had an interest in this residence matter. I remember in the public accounts committee two years ago when he was cross-examining-if I can use that phrase-the Hon. Brooke Claxton about it. At that time I felt he had the same viewpoint that I had. That year The Canada Council put 40 per cent, I believe, of its expenditure on the universities' side into residences. The next year, perhaps as a result of some of the protests we made in the committee and the complaints we made about this, it dropped to 7 per cent. The feeling of some of us on the committee was that the money The Canada Council was contributing on residences was really not as vital as its expenditures in other fields; more closely attached to the actual teaching process. It seems to me that this loan fund will remove from The Canada Council much of the onus it felt to provide residence funds.
There is one other problem regarding residences that I wish to mention. I will bring this matter up more particularly when we are going through the bill. I see no definition of "university" in the bill, and it bothers me from a general point of view. We very much need a residence at the lakehead college at Port Arthur, and I am sure that the new college under way at Sudbury will need a residence. This is because colleges in areas such as ours are drawing students from great distances. In many cases we have not the kind of boarding-house possibilities available in cities such as Toronto and Kingston.
I remember the big hullabaloo in Toronto a few years ago when the department of education decided to open a teachers' college on Pape avenue in east York. The prime reason for this decision was that this was an ideal boarding-house area, if nothing else. So this is an important factor for a teachers' college, indeed it is important to any kind of college. It is something that has to be considered, and in a region such as ours, where we draw students from an area about 500 miles long and several hundred miles deep, residence facilities could form a very integral part of the college system, an even more fundamental part than the residence can play at one of the major universities. Yet the lakehead college is not, properly speaking, a university and will not be such for a number of years.
National Housing Act
As I understand the term "university" it is a collation or collection of a number of faculties. There are some so-called universities in Canada that I do not think are properly such. I wonder whether it would not have been better if the minister had written right into this legislation some list-perhaps The Canada Council list-of recognized institutions of higher learning. As it stands at the present time many of the recognized institutions of higher learning could not qualify under the ordinary definition of the word "university", and that word is all I find in the act. I hope the minister will give some serious consideration to an amendment on this particular matter. It is one suggestion I wanted to mention in connection with university housing projects.
The other point I wanted to touch upon is pollution. I believe the Prime Minister was interested a number of years ago in the pollution problem; he was interested enough in this matter that he wanted to increase the penalties for any industries or communities that were creating pollution. In Ontario we have had instituted recently the Ontario water resources commission. This commission is making studies of pollution throughout the province. The Department of Public Works comes into this in the lakehead region in a way that has nothing to do with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation or this particular legislation but its reference to that matter is something that should be considered.
We have a pollution problem in the Kam-inistikwia river, the lakehead harbour and many of the surrounding beach areas of lake Superior. This pollution problem stems from the pulp and paper industry. The pollution is in two forms; there is a chemical solution there, of a phenol character, contained in the water. There is also a very high degree of debris and effluent in the Kaministikwia river. Is such debris pollution?
The department spends about $100,000 a year in dredging the Kaministikwia river. Some of the dredging is necessary, I am certain, because of the effluent that comes from one of the large paper mills there. Whose responsibility is it to check this particular type of pollution? The checks I have made would indicate that the Department of Public Works does not accept the responsibility for pollution in that sense, and yet that is the department in charge, as I understand it, of any amelioration in navigable waters; and it foots the bill for its removal.
Here we have a situation from a kind of pollution that I think can affect almost any kind of boreal region community; that is, the waste from a large pulp and paper mill. The alternative is for the provincial or municipal

National Housing Act authority officials, or the officials of the attorney general, to launch prosecutions under the Criminal Code, but this has never been very successful because of the sheer size and economic power of the pulp and paper groups. For this reason it would be a very brave municipality in Canada that would tackle them. Yet in Dryden, Port Arthur, and Fort William, to mention three examples, we have a genuine pollution problem caused by these industrial operations.
I would suggest to the minister that this particular type of pollution requires his attention, and such attention could even be hooked up with this particular bill. The main water pollution problems we have in the lakehead region are definitely, we think, nothing to do with municipal sewage at all; they have to do with industrial sewage from large plants whose effluent does not fall within the scope of municipal sewage at all. Perhaps the legislation could be so set up in a form, without any of this rebate business, that would encourage some of these large industries to instal the proper amount of pollution control or sewage system. I hate to suggest this kind of subsidization of private industry, because I have a hunch that the pulp and paper industry can well afford to handle this problem; but they do not seem ready to do so. The municipalities and the provinces seem to be frightened to tackle them head-on, and for that reason I bring this matter to the attention of the minister. Perhaps the minister could make a provision under this act to ensure loans to clear up this matter. Another way would be to use his authority in connection with navigable waters to actually police this type of pollution from another point of view altogether.
There is one other question which X would like to raise for the attention of the minister in connection with the municipal sewage problem. This, again, is a tendentious matter. In the city of Port Arthur we have a sectional sewage problem; that is, you can look at the city in terms of regions. As I understand our local set-up, if they are going to have a big, main sewer in a certain part of the city it is looked upon as a local improvement, to which the local taxpayers make a contribution; that is, they are assessed so much over a certain number of years until this expenditure is paid off.
It seems to me the way this is set up, without any safety rider, the federal government could be a means of introducing a kind of inequity into the municipal tax structure through this particular legislation. I will put it this way: supposing we have what we call a south end sewer project in the city of Port Arthur, and the people along that project know they are going to have to pay so much

of the cost, but because of this loan contribution plus the ensuing rebate from the federal government the cost would be much lower and the charge to the taxpayer would be much less? I say it is fine for the taxpayers in that particular part of the city, but what in the name of equity about the other taxpayers who have already provided for their sewer facilities, or who are now providing for them through local taxes particular to them and who are not going to be able to take advantage of this?
This is probably a minor point, but I should like to hear an explanation from the minister about it because in most of our larger cities it seems to me the definition of a main sewer does not necessarily mean one that serves an entire community; it could be serving a suburb of that community, and if it is going to affect tax structure in a favourable way for the taxpayers only in that area, what about the tax burden in other parts of the town? I do not want the minister to get the idea that I would like the whole contribution cancelled because of that point, but I should like to know whether he is considering the effect it may have on municipal taxation in this particular regard.
In conclusion, I should like to say that I was talking this week with a Canadian who was up here from a foreign capital. He had been stationed in Ottawa for some years and he said he could not get over the fact that despite this rather exciting speech from the throne and this forecast of a remarkable legislative program there did not seem to be much excitement around Ottawa because of it. Another person present observed that 150 or 200 members in this house were more concerned about whether their constituencies were safe or not than in becoming enthusiastic about the legislative program. However, I must say the number of speeches we have heard from the government benches would indicate that there is some reciprocity between looking at one's constituency to see whether it is safe or not and the making of a contribution to this debate and the fact that these members are supporting and congratulating the government for this legislation. It seems to me this is interesting to note.
The last point I want to make is that I have noticed one tendency which I hope is consistent throughout this session, and which I am sure is pleasing to those who sit on this side and observe the government benches closely. Almost everyone who has got up to congratulate the government has referred to the actions of the Conservative government. This is my fifth year, and at least we have a Conservative government now and not a Diefenbaker government. I rather welcome it as a member of the opposition.

Mr. Speaker, I feel badly every time the hon. member has to be reprimanded because I really do not think he knows any better. If he will just listen for a moment I will let him in on a little secret. In his area at least, the area of metropolitan Toronto, the problem is not one of down payment. Oh, oh.
Lack of confidence in the government.

In this case I think the two are synonymous. I do not say a lower down payment will have no effect. Obviously if the lowering of the down payment is made retroactive it will have some effect; it will help to mop up some of the unsold houses and help to clean up some of the mess the minister and his government have created, but the immediate effect has been dramatically exaggerated. For example, Mr. Speaker, I can tell the house from experience what happened last fall when the minister and his government did not realize soon enough

that the rates existing at that time cut off completely the flow of money into housing act loans.
The company with which I am associated had sold in advance a great number of houses. Some of the people who thought they were going to get houses could not because National Housing Act mortgages were not available, even though the government was building some with direct loans a stone's throw away which could not be sold. Some of them had sold their houses or given up the leases on their apartments and in order to meet what was a critical situation private financing was arranged at a higher interest rate. This was an emergency measure. The mortgages taken back were exactly the same as the National Housing Act mortgages in all respects as far as wording, repayment privileges and so forth were concerned. The difference was only one thing, namely the 1 per cent difference in the rate of interest. The minister, I am sure, would be interested to know that this cut the effective demand for housing by over 50 per cent. That was the dramatic effect the increase of 1 per cent had on the demand for housing.
The minister keeps talking about the little man. When he is talking about the little man I am not sure whether he means midgets or what he means. If he means the ordinary working man, the man who is in need of housing, that little man is the man who is most concerned and the most upset about the uncertainty in the Canadian economy at the present time, and he is the man who is so afraid of losing his job that he will not take on a large commitment at high interest rates which would last for a number of years.
Until these problems are solved, the government is not going to accomplish what it hopes to accomplish and what it has told the house it expects to be accomplished from the first part of this bill. This will mean a negligible number of new or additional starts this winter and an equally small number of new jobs.
The minister tells us that each new house employs five men for six months. He told us two men were on-site, two men off-site and one digging ditches for the sewers and water. If that is true, and I have no reason to doubt the minister's figures in this regard, the failure of the government's 1960 housing plans, which the minister now predicts will result in 110,000 starts instead of the 140,000 forecast by the minister of trade and commerce at the outset of the year, means that 150,000 more Canadians are without jobs. Thirty thousand less houses, 150,000 fewer jobs- those are the minister's own figures.
It certainly indicates that the government's 1960 plans were not sound. They were not

sound, or perhaps I should say they were nothing but sound, nothing but loud noises and soft markets. The government was warned, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member for Nipissing, the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Bourget) and I pointed out to the government that its 1960 plan would not work but the minister would not listen. No, he said it would. Things were going to turn out all right, he would achieve the starts which he predicted, and I think he had reduced his nominal forecast to 125,000 by that time.
When the minister told us that he was cutting back on direct government lending we said that the lending institutions would not take up the difference, particularly without the participation of the chartered banks. It is more than a guess to say that the great majority of municipalities in Canada will not be able to afford their share of the projects and the high cost of borrowing money discourages municipalities, and I think rightly so, from participating in very desirable but unjustifiably costly projects.
Though it is admittedly not the complete solution to the municipal problem, and I am convinced that there is no one solution for the municipal problem any more than there is for any of the other economic problems facing the country, surely a municipal grants assistance act designed both in form and in quantity to study and to provide realistic assistance to municipalities to meet their obligations in providing essential services to the municipalities, coupled with a municipal loan fund as suggested by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) as far back as 1958, whereby municipalities could borrow their necessary finance on a long term basis at reasonably attractive interest rates, would come far closer to hitting its mark than the do it yourself type of solution contained in this legislation in which, like most do it yourself kits, the one essential piece is missing, in this case, the financial ability of municipalities to participate in these schemes.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) seems to be a very difficult man to please these days. Yesterday he complained that we showed a lack of interest because we only put forward one speaker on the resolution and yet today when we put forward four speakers on second reading he accuses us of filibustering, and that in the face of the numerous speakers on the government side who have taken part in the debate.
The purpose of my intervention in the debate is mainly to reply to some of the statements made earlier by the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Pugh). I should like to begin by reminding the hon. member that this bill follows upon the adoption of a resolution which said that it was expedient to introduce this legislation in order to encourage the demand for housing. Why is it necessary to increase the demand for housing? If hon. members will give me the opportunity I will be only too glad to explain in the very greatest detail. Certainly it is not because there are not still many people who need houses. It cannot be because the needs of the people have been taken care of. That cannot be the reason why there is not sufficient demand at this time and why it is

National Housing Act
necessary for the government to take additional measures to encourage the demand. I hope that is clear to my hon. friend.
No, it is not; it is very confusing.

If there are still plenty of needs to be filled and in the face of all these need's it is necessary to introduce legislation to create a demand, then the main reason must be that private enterprise is not fulfilling its primary and normal function of providing for housing needs.
Join the C.C.F.

That must be the primary reason. If we pursue that line of thought we must come to the conclusion that we are now in some kind of economic emergency. Following upon the primary reason there is another reason which has been put forward by the minister and other speakers on the government side. According to them the secondary purpose is to provide jobs in order to take care of the unemployment problem.
There is no doubt that one of the most effective ways of creating jobs is to stimulate the construction industry. The construction industry is one of the most important, if not the most important, sectors of our national economy both from the standpoint of capital investment and from the standpoint of the number of people employed. Earlier this session we were told that the estimated capital expenditure of the construction industry this year was something like $7.5 billion which constituted about 25 per cent of our gross national product. In terms of jobs, the construction industry employs about 1.2 million people which is about 20 per cent of the working force. About half of these jobs are provided directly on the construction site, and the other half would be in related industries. It is obvious, therefore, that the injection of money into the construction industry is one of the most effective means of pump priming our economy.
The construction industry has two important divisions. One division is the government building program and the other is residential and institutional building. This bill which we are considering now refers only to the latter. I have gone through the supplementary estimates which were tabled a few days ago, and by making a rapid calculation I find that the estimates provide about $7 million for the acquisition of buildings and sites, which I take it is the government's contribution to this sector of the construction industry which is called the government building program.
This bill poses for all of us the fundamental question as to what should be the basic 
guiding principle of government policy in connection with housing in a free enterprise system. I have always understood that in a free enterprise economy such as we claim to support the primary function of government is to create the kind of climate in which private enterprise can flourish and take care of the needs of the people without too much government assistance or too much government interference. Apart from that, the area of governmental activity related to housing under a free enterprise system should be confined, for the most part, to those areas where free enterprise cannot operate at a profit and that includes such areas as slum clearance, the provision of houses for low income groups and for the still lower income groups who, perhaps, will never be able to acquire a home.
I am glad to see that this bill makes some provision for residential housing for universities because I think that falls within this particular category. Universities themselves are finding it difficult to finance the residential housing they need, and that puts them almost in the same boat as the small wage earner. But if we review the policy of this government since it has taken office there appears to be a radical departure from this traditional policy. It seems now that the primary policy towards housing is to use it as a stopgap, to turn it on and off in order to regulate the economy. It is turned on when jobs are scarce and turned off when jobs become plentiful. This is not the healthy atmosphere that the construction industry needs for its operation.
It does not happen, either.

My hon. friend says it does not happen, either. I believe my statement is borne out by the changes we have made in the housing act since this government has come to power. I would be only too glad to recapitulate them for him. In 1954 the Liberal government amended section 22 of the National Housing Act to provide public funds for housing up to $250 million. In 1957, when the present government took office, there had been a demand for about $100 million of this amount. The present government on taking office released the remaining $150 million. I give them credit for channelling that money mainly into houses for low income groups. By the end of 1957, however, the whole $250 million had been used up and in December, 1957 we amended section 22 again by raising the amount authorized from $250 million to $400 million; in May, 1958 we raised it from $400 million to $750 million; in March, 1959 we raised it again from $750 million to $1 billion. Last session, I do not recall the exact date, we raised it again from $1 billion

to $1.5 billion. This illustrates the stupendous increase in public funds made available for housing. The amount has risen in three years from $250 million to $1.5 billion. The hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Pugh) took great credit for this and used these figures to indicate what the present government has done to assist housing. If you look only at the surface it appears to be a valid argument.
However, I should like to point out to the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary that it does not matter whether you make available $1.5 million or $15 billion. This money has no effect unless there is a demand for it. I believe, in the present situation, we are conscious that there is no demand for this money which is available and we are trying to work out a sort of arrangement to induce people to make use of it. I want to expose the fallacy of this argument which has been used over and over again by hon. members opposite to create the impression that the Liberal government did nothing for housing and that everything has been done since the Conservatives took office.
I should like to point out that the real criterion is not how much money is available because, as I just said, whether you have $1 billion or $15 billion makes no difference if nobody is going to use it. The real criterion is the number of houses built in a year and that is the point in which we Liberals are interested. What is this legislation going to mean in terms of an actual increase in the number of houses started and completed?
In 1955, under the Liberal government, when there were only $250 million available, 138,276 houses were built. Today, with $1,500 million available, the best the Tories can produce is 100,000 houses. That is the measure; that is the real criteria-not the dollars available, but the number of houses actually built. A better criteria still is how well the economy is functioning. I am not condemning, blaming or criticizing the government for introducing this measure. We are in a situation where something has to be done.
We are doing it too.

Yes, and we are quite willing to help you do it. The only blame which attaches to the government is to what extent they themselves have created the situation which has brought this about; the contribution they have made, by mismanagement, poor fiscal policies, tight money and an atmosphere of confusion and uncertainty in which it is impossible for private enterprise to function normally and fill the needs of the people as it should do in a free enterprise economy.
I support very strongly the new features introduced in this bill, the features that deal
National Housing Act
with pollution, with university residential housing and aid to municipalities. But I think the figures I have outlined today should cause free enterprise to just pause and consider what is happening.
As the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) himself said-and I think the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) also-the government cannot do everything. I think it behooves private enterprise to examine itself to see whether it is fulfilling and carrying out to the fullest possible extent the responsibilities which devolve upon it in a free enterprise economy. The only alternative to free enterprise is socialism. If free enterprise is not prepared to do everything in its power, if is wants to leave the initiative in everything to the government or if it forces the government into a position where the government has no choice but to take action, then free enterprise will have only itself to blame if some day it finds that we have been transformed into a socialist economy.

On Monday we will have second reading of Bill No. C-40 dealing with small business. If that is completed we will proceed with technical and vocational training at whatever stage it might be, whether in the resolution stage or second reading. Monday, under

Business of the House
the old rule, would normally be a private members' day, but under the amended rules we have the privilege of using that Monday for government business.
The forecast for the rest of the week appears to be as follows. On Tuesday, in response to the request of the Leader of the Opposition for an early opportunity to discuss international affairs, supported by the member for Vancouver East-who suggested that there should be the earliest possible opportunity for discussing this matter-I am suggesting that we have a debate on external affairs.
On Wednesday we will deal with government business. I hope we can then set up the standing committees of the house and various special committees, some of which commenced their work last session and did not complete it, such as the committee on rules and procedure, the committee on research, the Indian affairs committee-which is a joint committee with the other place- and the committee on broadcasting. Thursday of next week would be private members' day.

I wish to ask a question with particular reference to the minister's mention of the one-day debate on external affairs. The point of view of this group is that one day is not sufficient; it is inconclusive; very often it gives no opportunity to members other than the leaders to speak in the debate. We would ask the government to consider a two-day debate on external affairs.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I would like to point out to the house leader that I have some doubt whether the Leader of the Opposition will be here. I cannot say that he will; I know that he will be away tomorrow and again on
Monday because he has several engagements, and it may well be that he will not arrive in time.
I thought he wanted to get on with the business of the house.
That is right; he wants to get on with the business of the house.
To meet the unemployment crisis.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am trying to be as friendly as I can in this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: So am I.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I was not going to suggest anything; I was simply bringing it to the attention of the house leader. I am sure that if the Leader of the Opposition is here he will be quite prepared to take part in the debate. But it may well be he will not arrive by 2.30.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: As in other sessions, we have tried to make arrangements to suit all parties. I introduced this by saying "the forecast for next week runs pretty much as follows". We may have to make certain adjustments. I think we could perhaps consider this tomorrow through the usual channels.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am not asking for any postponement of the debate. I would like to leave it this way, that I will communicate with him tomorrow if I can, and then perhaps I can speak to the house leader.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
That is fine.
It being six minutes after ten o'clock, the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.

Friday, November 25, 1960
